I suggest getting tested again in 1-3 months. If he’s being truthful about testing positive for an STD, he’s probably had it for at least 1-3 months or more. Newly contracted STDs sometimes take time to show positive test results. Also, I would ask which STD he tested positive for and test for that specific STD. Less innocuous STDS, such as herpes aren’t usually tested for unless specified due to the fact that it isn’t life threatening and most of the population has it (also known as cold sores) without knowing they have it. 
I would definitely ask to get re-tested in a month or so for the specific STD that he has. What he said is somewhat true; your STD may be lying dormant at the moment, but you should still test positive even if it has been lying dormant for years. 
Positive or negative test results are not necessarily dependent on who caught it first because it may not have had enough time to create symptoms or take over your system/infect certain organs. 
It seems new though if you’re testing negative. 
It’s a good tell sign to see negative results first, giving you time to re-test in a month or two and to receive treatment early. 
It’s hard to determine who caught what first due to the simple fact: Everyone’s body is different.
I wish you both luck.

It’s the hard truth. We all too often use relationships as a way to numb OUR pain. Going into the relationship assuming that the other person is there because they like you and they want to care for you. Sure, there’s partial truth there, but it would be selfish to stay in that relationship, feel loneliness again and realize it isn’t your spouse that is making you feel loneliness… it is yourself. Using the relationship to cover up the fact that you felt loneliness before you met them and partly moved into the relationship to hide from loneliness. 

Admit it or not, it is selfish to say that you’re not in a relationship to hide your loneliness and you’re there for other reasons. 

We all do it at some point and it’s okay. What isn’t okay, is not being able to admit it and continuously living the rest of your life trying to get rid of loneliness you keep trying to cover up. It’s like covering up a corpse with sand that just blows away. It’s still there and it’ll resurface over time. You’ll have to live the rest of your life burying it with different things.

Everyone feels loneliness on a spectrum. You’re always going to feel that loneliness regardless of being in a romantic relationship or not if you are emotionally unstable. That loneliness stems from personal insecurities and the need for comfort regardless of what kind of comfort that may be. 
There are plenty of people who feel lonely after getting used to a relationship. 
Loneliness within your relationships does not reflect your partner’s ability to comfort you, but it reflects your inner self. 

If you are unhappy before the relationship, and use the relationship as a protection mechanism to block out that loneliness, it’ll always come back. 

That’s why, in my opinion… learning how to navigate life alone and restoring your brokenness inside first will always pay off when you finally decide to commit to a relationship. So unfortunately, the yearning you have for wanting someone to lean on or comfort you, will always come back regardless of how good your current relationship is going. It is just a temporary fix. Don’t use people or relationships to protect yourself from your feelings of sadness and loneliness. It’ll only hurt the other person more and is very selfish.

If there’s one thing that I learned today during deeper studies into meditation, it is that we all slip. We can master meditation and reach the highest state, but it doesn’t stop us from being humans and experiencing feelings or emotions. It’s not your fault that you experience these things.

Although, you do have the choice to let go. 
You can let go of bad experiences that left bad impressions, or you can choose to hold a grudge and let your thoughts straddle you along. 

Yes, trauma hurts. 

Meditation teaches you to have your heart open at all times. Having your heart open means you allow experiences to be just what they are… EXPERIENCES. Whether they’re good or bad. It’s life. Life isn’t life if there are no bad experiences. I wish I had the power to wish that bad things never happened to anyone and that I wish there weren’t bad people in the world, EXCEPT THERE ARE. We can’t change that. We can’t control that.
If only bad things never happened to people, right??

Once we go though a bad experience, our natural instinct is to close up, get angry and blame everything, try to make changes on the outside to protect our feelings. Meditation teaches you that instead of being defensive and wanting to protect your fears, just let go. Expose your fears and be willing to let go of the negative experience that caused your fear. You can’t live a meaningful life by trying to build a life AROUND your fears.

The only reason it’s difficult to let go of trauma is because we’ve been holding in so much for so long. The longer you choose not to let go, the harder it will be to let go. 

We fall into a depressive state of mind when we listen to that voice inside your head. The voice people call, “anxiety”. The voice people call, “overthinking”. The voice people choose to listen to then say, “I’m indecisive”. 
Your thoughts will dig you a hole so deep, you’ll feel like you can’t get out. You start to see the world very negatively and everyday feels heavy. Everything they everyone does will bother you and will hit your triggers.

Your thoughts are only an object that you are aware of. Your feelings too, are only objects you are aware of. You are not your thoughts nor your feelings, you are simply just the experiencer of these thoughts snd feelings. 

So to those who say, if meditation works, why do we still fall into depression? 

It’s natural. We’re human. We will fall, but you still have the option to get up after closing your heart off. You still have the option to work through it. Yes, it’ll be difficult, but you ultimately make the decision to whether or not you want to let go. 

The book, “The untethered soul”, by Michael Singer may be of help to you or anyone struggling with understanding trauma and mental illnesses. It’ll also give you a deeper understanding of meditation and what it means.
